t: And borrows from others. Takes a loan.
The garment on his shoulder. His clothing.
All of it at once, one time. In one coin and at one time.

The rapist and the seducer. One who has relations with a virgin girl by force or who seduced the minor, and the Torah fined them to pay fifty silver (Deuteronomy 22:29, Exodus 22:15-16; and see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:1).

And one who slanders. One who marries a woman and falsely claims that she was not a virgin when she married him. The Torah fined him to pay one hundred silver (Deuteronomy 22:19; and see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 3:1).
And one whose ox kills a slave. A person whose ox killed a slave or maidservant. The Torah fined him to pay thirty silver (Exodus 21:32, and see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 11:1).
A barley grain. A grain of barley (its weight is 1/20 of a gram).
And the Sages already added to it. They added to the weight of the Torah shekel and adapted it to the weight of the sela in their days.
A sela was four dinars and a dinar is six ma'ah. It turns out that the shekel, after the Sages added to its measure, is twenty-four ma'ah. But before that the shekel was twenty ma'ah.
And the ma'ah is what was called gerah in the days of Moses our teacher. As stated in the Torah in connection with the mitzvah of the half-shekel: "twenty gerah to the shekel" (Exodus 30:13).
From the holy shekel. From the shekel mentioned in the Torah.
And freed slaves. Freed Canaanite slaves, who have the status of Israelites in every respect (Hilchot Issurei Biah 12:17).
And if they gave, it is accepted from them. Although they are not obligated.

But gentiles who gave a half-shekel, it is not accepted from them. For the half-shekels are designated for communal offerings, and a gentile has no share in the communal offerings (similarly see below 4:8; and see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:2 that no offerings at all are accepted from them except a voluntary burnt offering).

A minor for whom his father began to give a half-shekel no longer stops. For "we say to him: since you gave a shekel for him last year and obligated him in this mitzvah, give for him always until he becomes a man and do not stop" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 1:3).
Only while the Temple stands. When the Temple exists, since the shekels are for the needs of the offerings and the Temple (below 4:1).
On the first of Adar. A month before the chamber donation, which is done on the first of Nisan (below 2:5).
They announce concerning the shekels. Agents of the court announce in all the cities of Israel about giving the half-shekels, so that they will be ready to give them on time (ibid. 1:1).
The money changers. Currency exchangers, who customarily place their coins on the table before them.
In every single province. In all the cities of Israel, except Jerusalem, where they sit from the twenty-fifth of the month.
In the Temple. In Jerusalem (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 1:3).
His pledge. His collateral.

Even his garment. And there is no obligation to return to him the day garment or night garment, as with other collateral (see Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 3:5, and see also Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 3:14).
Even though it is his practice to give. For example, a minor for whom his father began to give a half-shekel (see above halacha 7).
Or he is going to give. For example, a minor who will come of age close to the first of Nisan, or a slave who will be freed.
We do not take collateral from him. Since he is not yet obligated by law.
For the sake of peace. Because the kohanim thought they were exempt from paying (see Mishnah Shekalim 1:4), and so as not to harm their honor (Yerushalmi ibid. 1:3).
In every single province. In all the towns outside Jerusalem.
The bottom of the chest. The base of the chest.
Like a shofar. Round and curved (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 6:1).

And it would not be possible to take from them comfortably. So that it would be possible to remove coins from the chest only by turning it over, because of thieves who would put in their hand as if to donate and take coins from the chest (ibid.).
Who did not give a shekel. Who did not give the half-shekel.
And in the Temple. In the Temple, in the courtyard.
For the shekels of this year. For the half-shekel of this year, which goes to the chamber donation.
For the shekels of the past year. For the half-shekel of one who did not donate in previous years.

For anyone who owes an offering of two turtledoves or two young pigeons etc.. One who is obligated to offer a pair of birds, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering, for his atonement, such as a zav and a zavah or a poor woman after childbirth (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3); the pair of birds is called a "kin." The kohanim would empty the shofar chest every day and offer kinim according to the number of coins (see ibid. 1:12). Likewise, the kohanim would empty the other shofar chests and use the coins for their designated purpose (see Tosefta Shekalim 3:2-6).
One who owes only a bird burnt offering. For example, one who vowed to offer a bird burnt offering.
Wood for the arrangement. For the fire arrangement on the altar; an individual may bring it as a voluntary gift (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1).
For frankincense. One of the ingredients of the incense; it too comes as a voluntary gift and is offered on the altar (ibid.).
For one who donated gold for the kapporet. For the renovation of the kapporet or for the plating of the Holy of Holies (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 6:5, and see Tosefta ibid. 3:6).
And there was money left over. He had change left after buying the animal.
The kinim of zavim, zavot and women after childbirth. The "kin" that they must bring for their atonement.
The offerings of a nazir. That a nazir is obligated to bring when he became impure during his nazirite days or that he brings at the completion of his nazirite days.
The guilt offering of a metzora. The offering the metzora brings upon his purification.
And it is a condition of the court regarding all the surpluses that they be offered as an animal burnt offering. Even though he consecrated the money for the sake of another offering.
For all the money found in the last six chests. These are money left over from the various offerings.
And their hides belong to the kohanim like all other hides. The hides of the most holy offerings belong to the kohanim (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:19).

And they may exchange them for gold dinars because of the burden of the road. They are permitted to convert the half-shekels into larger coins so that the small coins will not weigh them down on the way to Jerusalem.
Nine se'ah. About 64 liters.

And this which is inside the boxes is called the chamber donation. For the money inside the boxes they would set aside into small boxes ("donating the chamber") for the purchase of the offerings, as explained in the next halacha.
Three times a year they donate the chamber. The reason for this will be explained below, halacha 8.
They donate the chamber. They set aside money from the large boxes and put it into smaller boxes from which they take the money to use it.
And on the first of Tishrei, before the festival. Of Rosh Hashanah, which is the twenty-ninth of Elul.
Atzeret. The festival of Shavuot.
To be supplied from them. To use them to buy offerings and the like.
And on the first of Nisan they donate from the new donation. From the new shekels, and not from the shekels that were brought the previous year.
And he donates first from the one large box etc.. Here is detailed the order of filling the small boxes from the large ones at each of the periods.

Until it turns out that he has donated the first, second and third small ones from each and every one of the large ones. From each large box they filled each of the small boxes, so that from each large box the shekels would be donated on behalf of all of Israel, since each of the small boxes is donated on behalf of a particular portion of Israel, as below, halacha 8 (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 3:4).
When he donates these three boxes. When he fills the small boxes from the large boxes.
He donates the first. The small box on which the letter alef is written.
On behalf of the surrounding walled cities adjacent to it. The cities surrounding the Land of Israel near it.

And on behalf of all Israel. On behalf of all Israel who are in these walled cities. Likewise for the third box, "and on behalf of the rest of all Israel," he means the rest of all Israel in all these countries, since each box is donated on behalf of a portion of Israel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 3:4). It is possible that its meaning is that when he donates the second box he includes also the people of the Land of Israel for whom he donated in the first box, and in the third box he includes the rest of Israel for whom he donated in the first two boxes.
On behalf of what has been collected in the chamber. Even though it was not put into the three large boxes ("the remainders of the chamber").
And on behalf of what has been collected but has not yet reached the chamber. The shekels from distant countries that are on the way.
And on behalf of what is yet to be collected. From those who have not yet given their shekels.
Atonement for all Israel. So that everyone will have a share in the communal offerings that are bought with this money.
In a garment in which one can hide money. For example, a garment that has a seam or a pocket.
In a tefillah. Tefillin.
In an amulet. A parchment on which they write charms and which is covered with leather; in all of these money can be hidden.
Hasty for wealth. One who loves and pursues money.
Everyone needs half-shekels. For one must give the half-shekel in a single coin (see above 1:1).

Therefore, when a person would go to the money changer etc.. Because the half-shekel coin is in demand at this time, one who breaks a shekel into two halves in order to use them for his own needs pays the money changer a fee for the exchange.
Therefore, two who gave a shekel etc.. Therefore two who gave a whole shekel must pay this fee to the Temple treasury (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 1:6).
And the obligated person gave through the exempt person. On behalf of the exempt person.
He is exempt from the kolbon. For the half-shekel that he gave for them is an act of piety, and therefore they exempted him from the kolbon (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 1:6).
Kohanim are exempt from the kolbon. Just as we do not take collateral from them for the shekels for the sake of peace (above 1:10), so too they exempted them from the kolbon.
When their means allow. When they are able to repay.

They are exempt from the kolbon. Since the coin comes out of one purse of partnership money, it does not constitute a combination of two separate halves, and therefore they are not liable for the kolbon (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 1:6).
In what case is this said?. That partners are exempt.

And the form of the coins changed. The original coins that each one brought into the partnership are no longer there, and therefore the coins before us are defined as partnership money and as one purse.

But if this one brought his coins and that one brought his coins and they mixed them, and the coins have not yet changed etc.. In this case the coins are considered the money of several individuals located in one place (see Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 4:3), and the law is like that of two who gave a shekel for both of them (above halacha 1).
And after some time they divided and became partners again, they are liable for the kolbon. Because they have not yet traded with the money of the new partnership, and these coins have not changed.
To the Temple treasury. To the Temple for the purpose of the half-shekel.

He is liable for two kolbonim. One kolbon because he brought a whole shekel and must pay an exchange fee like anyone who brings a whole shekel, and one kolbon for the half-shekel he received from the Temple treasury.
At the time when they used to give two dinars for the half-shekel. See above 1:2-3.
Which is one in twelve of a dinar. For a dinar has six ma'ah, so the kolbon is one part in twenty-four of the half-shekel.
And the kolbon was never given at less than this. For the measure of two dinars is the minimum standard measure for giving a half-shekel.
They are not like the shekels. And they are not given to the chamber donation as is done with the shekels (above 2:4).
Rather the money changers set them aside by themselves. Separately from the shekels.
Until the Temple treasury is supplied from them. Until the treasurers use it as needed for the purposes of the Temple treasury.
He is liable for its safekeeping. And he must pay a second time.
Until he hands it over to the treasurer. For from the moment it passed into the ownership of the Temple treasury, the giver is not responsible for it.

If he is an unpaid guardian etc.. If he did not receive payment for the guarding, he is an unpaid guardian who is exempt from responsibility in case of theft or loss but must swear to the people of the town that he guarded properly (Hilchot Sechirut 1:2, Hilchot She'elah UFikadon 4:1).

And they give their shekels a second time. For they should have sent the money with a paid guardian, and since they did not do so, it is as if they lost the money themselves (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 2:1).

Since we are paying, we do not want the agent to swear, for he is trustworthy to us. For an unpaid guardian may pay for a deposit that was lost from him and then be released from the oath (Hilchot She'elah UFikadon 6:1), and they want to exempt him from the oath because they are paying.

It is an ordinance of the Sages that the Temple treasury is not released without an oath. So that people not come to treat Temple funds lightly (see also Hilchot Sechirut 2:2, Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 5:1).
And they do not count toward another year for them. Toward the half-shekel obligation of the following year.

In the hand of a paid guardian. One who guards another's deposit for payment is liable for theft and loss, and if it was due to circumstances beyond his control he swears to the owner that it was lost through circumstances beyond his control and is exempt from paying (Hilchot Sechirut 1:2).
After the donation was donated. The first donation, which is donated on the first of Nisan.

For the one donating donates on behalf of what has been collected and what is yet to be collected. As above 2:8, and therefore this money is considered money that reached the ownership of the Temple treasury, and the community is not responsible for it.
Through him. For him.
By himself. For himself, and not for his friend who sent him.
So that they will not take collateral from him. For one who does not give a half-shekel has collateral taken from him (above 1:9).
If the donation was donated. Before he gave the shekel to the Temple treasury.

The weigher committed me'ilah. And he must pay principal and an added fifth to the Temple treasury and bring a me'ilah guilt offering (see Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3), in addition to his obligation to his friend.

And it turns out that this one saved himself with Temple money. The me'ilah here is not because he fulfilled the mitzvah of the half-shekel with Temple money, for mitzvot were not given for benefit, but because by this giving he saved himself from the collateral (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 2:2).

And if the donation was not donated, he did not commit me'ilah. For before the chamber donation the money is not yet considered in the ownership of the Temple treasury (see also Hilchot Me'ilah 6:13).
He has fulfilled his obligation. Because he acquired the stolen or robbed item following the owners' despair and the change of the item's ownership.
And he is liable to pay the owners double. In a case where he stole and witnesses testified to it (Hilchot Genevah 1:4).
Or to add a fifth. In a case where he robbed and swore falsely and afterwards confessed, in which case he pays principal and a fifth (Hilchot Gezelah 7:1).
From the Temple treasury. From money that was consecrated for Temple maintenance.
When they are supplied from it. When they buy an animal with the donated money and offer it (see Hilchot Me'ilah 6:12).
From the money of second tithe. The redemption money of second tithe, with which one buys food in Jerusalem and eats it there (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1-2).
He shall eat the equivalent in Jerusalem. He should buy produce worth the value of this money in order to eat it in Jerusalem (compare ibid. 7:17).
From the proceeds of the Sabbatical year. Money from the sale of Sabbatical-year produce, with which he buys food and eats it with Sabbatical sanctity (Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 6:6-7).
He shall eat the equivalent with Sabbatical sanctity. See also ibid. 6:10.
If it belonged to an apostate city. A city most of whose inhabitants were led astray to worship idols, and which is burned along with all the property in it (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:6).
He has done nothing. Since this money is destined for burning and benefit from it is forbidden, it is considered as if he gave nothing.
One who sets aside his shekel. Designated a coin for the half-shekel and has not yet given it.
It is not sanctified. And it may be used for ordinary purposes, since a consecration made in error is not a consecration (Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 6:34).
The last one is not sanctified. For the last shekel was given in error.
And the second is a surplus of shekels. And it may be used for ordinary purposes, as in the next halacha.
He set aside his shekel and died. Before he gave it.
It falls to the voluntary offerings. And burnt offerings of animals are offered from it (above 2:3).
One who takes coins in his hand and says, "These are for my shekel". He set them aside for giving the half-shekel, and they turn out to be more than the measure of a half-shekel.
A purse. A wallet.

For a surplus of shekels is ordinary. For the obligation is to give only a half-shekel and no more than that, and therefore the sanctity of the half-shekel does not take effect on the additional coins.
Between a chest of shekels and a chest of voluntary offerings. For details of the chests see above 2:5.

Because the entire voluntary offering goes to burnt offerings for the fires. For from the voluntary-offering money they take burnt offerings, which are entirely consumed. And because the sanctity of a burnt offering is more stringent, the doubtful coins fall to the voluntary offering.
And the shekels are used for burnt offerings and for other things. That are not a burnt offering, or that do not go up on the altar at all (see below 4:1).

If they were found between wood and frankincense, they fall to the frankincense. For frankincense is an offering whereas wood is merely an aid for offering the offerings, and therefore frankincense is more stringent.

Between kinim and young pigeons for a burnt offering, they fall to young pigeons for a burnt offering. For the sanctity of young pigeons for a burnt offering, which is entirely consumed, is more stringent than that of kinim, part of which is for a burnt offering and part for a sin offering.
In all of them we follow the nearest. The nearest chest to the coins.
And all the money found on the Temple Mount is ordinary. And we do not worry that it is Temple money.

For the treasurer does not take money out of the chamber donation until he redeems it for the animals he buys for the offerings. The treasurer takes ordinary money and buys animals with it, and afterwards transfers the sanctity from the money to the animals (redemption) and releases this money to ordinary status; therefore there is no concern that it is Temple money.
The chamber donation. The half-shekel money that was set aside into the boxes (see above 2:4-6).
The daily temidim. The morning and afternoon tamid offerings that one is commanded to offer every day.
And the additional offerings. The offerings brought in addition to the temidim on Shabbat, new moons and festivals.
And their libations. The flour, oil and wine that come with the offerings.
And the salt with which all the offerings are salted. For it is a mitzvah to salt every offering before it is brought up on the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).

And likewise the wood, if they did not bring wood. For there were fixed days for certain families to bring wood for the arrangement on the altar (Hilchot Kli HaMikdash 6:9), and an individual may also donate wood for the arrangement (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:1); when they did not bring wood and did not find other wood, it had to be bought.

And the incense and the wages of those who make it. For making the incense is a complex matter known only to certain individuals (Hilchot Kli HaMikdash 2:2), and they received their wages from the Temple.
And the showbread. The twelve loaves that one is commanded to arrange on the table in the Temple every Shabbat.
And the omer. Offered on the sixteenth of Nisan (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 7:3).
And the two loaves. Offered on the festival of Shavuot (ibid. 8:1).
And the red heifer. Whose ashes are used to purify from corpse impurity.

And the scapegoat and the crimson thread that is tied between its horns. The goat sent to Azazel on Yom Kippur, and a piece of wool dyed red is tied between its horns (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 3:4).

The bull for a matter hidden from the community and the goats of idolatry. When the court erred and ruled mistakenly regarding one of the mitzvot, each tribe brings a bull; and if they erred and ruled it permitted regarding idolatry, each tribe brings a goat (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:5, Hilchot Shegagot 12:1).
At the outset they collect for them. A special collection is held for them, and the chamber donation is not used.

The curtains of the Sanctuary are made as part of the structure. The curtains that separated the Sanctuary from the Holy of Holies and served as part of the building's partitions (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 4:2); therefore money consecrated for Temple repair is used for them.
The curtains of the gates. Curtains that hung at the gates of the courtyard and at the entrance of the Sanctuary and the Ulam (Hilchot Kli HaMikdash 7:17).
From the surplus of libations. Profits of the Temple treasury resulting from price differences in buying libations and selling them.
And in Hilchot Kli HaMikdash VeHa'Ovdim Bo it will be explained what the surplus of libations is. There, 7:13.

Those found in Jerusalem or outside it near it are brought as burnt offerings. Those found in Jerusalem or its vicinity without owners; because we suspect they were consecrated for the altar, burnt offerings must be brought with their value.
As will be explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 6:18.

And likewise a gentile who sent his burnt offering from another country and did not send with it the value of the libations. Even though a gentile who donates a burnt offering does not bring libations with it, if he did send the value of libations, they are bought with that money. And if he did not send money with it, its libations are offered from the chamber donation (based on Mi'ar HaKorbanot and Even HaAzel, Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:5).
A convert who died and left behind sacrifices. Because a convert has no heirs; but if he has heirs, or an Israelite died and left behind sacrifices, the libations come from his heirs' estate.
If he has libations. That he set aside libations during his lifetime for the offering.
And they did not appoint another in his place. But if they appointed another in his place, the other kohen is obligated to bring the chavitin (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 3:20-22).
The chavitin. The meal offering that the High Priest offers every day (see ibid. 3:18).
Inspectors of blemishes in Jerusalem. Those who examine the offerings for blemishes.
And those who teach them the laws of kemitzah. How to take the handful of the meal offering (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 13:13).

And women who raise their sons for the red heifer. Women who kept their sons from ever becoming impure with corpse impurity so that they could sprinkle on the kohen who burns the heifer (see Hilchot Parah 2:7).
That they set. That they fix.

In a Sabbatical year, which is ownerless. Grain growing in the seventh year is defined as ownerless since it is permitted to be eaten by everyone. For this reason it is necessary to guard the new grain for the bringing of the omer and the two loaves.
The aftergrowth. Grain that grows by itself in the Sabbatical year (Hilchot Shemitah VeYovel 4:1).

The omer and the two loaves, which come only from the new grain. For the omer offering, offered on the sixteenth of Nisan, and the two loaves, offered on Shavuot, must be brought only from new grain (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 6:15).
Men of force. Violent people.
So that everyone will keep away from the place that these are guarding. For by taking wages the matter will become known and others will refrain from taking them.

Correctors of books in Jerusalem. The correctors of the accurate Torah scroll that was in the Temple, from which other Torah scrolls were corrected and amended (commentary of Rabbenu Meshullam on Yerushalmi Shekalim 4:2, and see Mishnah Mo'ed Katan 3:4). Some explained that it refers to a Torah scroll from which the High Priest read on Yom Kippur and the king at the Hakhel assembly (commentary of a disciple of the Rashbash on Yerushalmi ibid.). Others explain that since a person is forbidden to leave an uncorrected book in his house, the Sages ordained to pay the correctors from the chamber donation (Rashi, Ketubot 106a).

They would build a ramp from the Temple Mount to the Mount of Anointing. A raised path, like a bridge, leading from the Temple to the Mount of Olives, on which those engaged in burning the heifer walked so as not to become impure (see Hilchot Parah 3:1).

On which they take out the scapegoat. That they send it to Azazel on Yom Kippur. They made a ramp for it because the Babylonians used to pull out the hair of the one who sent it so that he would hurry on his way (Mishnah Yoma 6:4).
From the remainders of the chamber. The shekels in excess of the shekels placed in the boxes (see above 2:4). [Note: in the Commentary on the Mishnah, the Rambam vocalizes it everywhere as shirei.]
The aqueduct in Jerusalem. Maintenance of the channel that supplied water to the residents of Jerusalem.
A resident alien. A gentile living in the Land of Israel who accepted upon himself to observe the seven Noahide commandments (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:6).

The surplus of the chamber donation and likewise the surplus of the remainders of the chamber. The shekels left over from the previous year's shekels after the new donation was already donated on the first of Nisan.
For it is a condition of the court regarding all the surpluses that they be offered as animal burnt offerings. See also above 2:3.

Summer fruit of the altar. Burnt offerings brought as an addition to the obligatory offerings, called "summer fruit of the altar" after the summer fruits that are eaten as dessert at the end of a meal (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 4:4).
They take out what is fitting for them from the sanctified property of Temple maintenance. They use money consecrated for repair of the building and its needs.

But Temple maintenance does not take out what is fitting for it from the sanctified property of the altar. From money consecrated for the purpose of offering sacrifices, since the sanctity of this money is more stringent and one raises up in sanctity and does not lower.
And if the new one did not come. The half-shekels of the new donation did not arrive.
They redeem them and they go out to ordinary status. They sell these animals, and their sanctity passes to the money and the animals are considered ordinary.

Even though they are unblemished. Although generally sanctified animals are redeemed only if a blemish occurred in them (see Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 5:11), in this case it is a condition of the court that even without a blemish they go out to ordinary status by sale.
With which they provide summer fruit for the altar. That they buy animals with this money and offer burnt offerings from them, as above, halacha 9.
With the surplus of the incense. For the incense too is taken from the chamber donation money (above halacha 1), and what is left over of it is sacred.
When the first of Nisan arrives. And one must buy incense from the new donation.

They redeem it for the wages of the craftsmen etc.. They set aside money from the chamber donation and designate it for the craftsmen who make the incense, and thereby this money goes out to ordinary status (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 4:5). Afterwards they redeem the sanctity of the surplus incense onto the money and buy with it burnt offerings for the "summer fruit of the altar." The incense is given to the craftsmen as their wages, and afterwards they buy it from them with the money of the new donation for the incense of the new year (and the reason they do not give the incense to the craftsmen as their wages at the outset is that Temple property is not redeemed onto labor but onto money - Hilchot Me'ilah 8:3).
